list.listitem: Consider acute paronychia in patients presenting with tenderness, erythema, swelling, and sometimes fluctuance or induration of the proximal or lateral nail folds. Chronic paronychia is characterized by symptoms present for 6 weeks or more and is associated with loss of cuticle, nail fold hypertrophy, and nail plate changes. C

Warm soaks or compresses, with or without topical antibiotics, can be used for acute paronychia without abscess or cellulitis. If topical antibiotics are used, addition of a topical corticosteroid may decrease time to symptom resolution. B
Oral antibiotics are generally not required after successful incision and drainage of acute paronychia with abscess. B
Topical steroids are more effective than systemic antifungals in the treatment of chronic paronychia. B
Chronic paronychia is treated by avoidance of irritants and treating inflammation with topical steroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors. C
Avoidance of inciting agents such as irritants, manipulation, and excessive moisture may reduce recurrences. C

background.definition: Paronychia is inflammation of the proximal and/or lateral nail folds. Acute paronychia is typically infectious and presents for less than 6 weeks after disruption of the nail-fold barrier. Chronic paronychia is present for 6 weeks or longer and is usually an irritant or allergic dermatitis caused by repeated barrier disruption, moisture, and exposure to irritants; secondary microbial colonization may occur.

list.listitem: There is paucity of data on the incidence of paronychia but it is recognized to be one of the most common infections of hands and feet.
Paronychia are three times more common in women.
Middle-aged females are at the highest risk of infection.

Paronychia can result from finger sucking, nail biting, manicures, excessive moisture, and contact with irritants, as well as drugs such as retinoids, protease inhibitors, epidermal growth factor inhibitors (eg, cetuximab, erlotinib) 2 to 4 months after starting treatment and antiretrovirals (eg, indinavir, lamivudine) 2 to 12 months after starting treatment.

Acute paronychia: can result from direct contact with mouth flora as well as during nail trauma that disrupts the cuticle, which is a seal between the cuticle and the proximal nail fold. Common bacteria isolated are Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, Pseudomonas, and anaerobes. Approximately 50% of cases of acute paronychias are polymicrobial, resulting from mixed aerobic and anaerobic infections.

Chronic paronychia usually results from repeated exposure to moisture, irritants, or allergens, causing loss of the cuticle and disruption of the nail-fold barrier. Candida and bacteria may be isolated, but they usually represent colonization rather than the primary cause. Antifungal therapy is generally not indicated unless there is confirmed candidiasis or concomitant onychomycosis.

The nail plate, directly over the nail bed, is surrounded laterally and proximally by nail folds (collectively referred to as the perionychium) and distally by the hyponychium. The eponychium, an outgrowth of the proximal nail fold that serves as a barrier between the nail plate and skin, protects against irritants and pathogens. Disruption of this barrier can lead to paronychia following exposure to pathogens and irritants.

Paronychia recurrence may be reduced by the avoidance of irritants, excessive moisture, nail biting, finger sucking, and trimming cuticles. Recommend applying moisturizing lotion after handwashing and keeping nails trimmed. C

Counsel individuals who wash hands constantly or whose hands are chronically wet (eg, bartenders, dishwashers, chefs) to use cotton gloves under vinyl or nitrile gloves when their hands are exposed to water, moisture, or irritants. C
Maintain good glycemic control in diabetic patients. C

Consider paronychia based on history such as minor trauma, finger sucking, or chronic irritant exposure. Suspect acute paronychia in the patient with tenderness, erythema, swelling, and sometimes fluctuance or induration of the proximal or lateral nail folds. C
Chronic paronychia is often accompanied by loss of cuticle, nail fold hypertrophy, and nail plate changes (eg, discoloration, hypertrophy, onycholysis), with symptoms present for 6 weeks or more. C
Culture of expressed fluid should not be routinely performed, as results seldom impact management. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Separation of nail plate from underlying structures, rarely associated with inflammation
Chronic eczema of the hands can cause ridges, discoloration, and/or nail thickening.
Vesicles, severe pain, possible HSV exposure, fever or malaise; avoid incision and drainage because this can worsen viral spread or delayed healing.
Possible plaques in other areas of the body, nail pitting, hyperkeratosis (acrodermatitis continua variant)

Persistent, single-digit, recurrent, atypical, or treatment-resistant nail-fold inflammation should prompt consideration of squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, or other nail-unit tumor; biopsy if concerning.
Closed space infection of fingertip pulp
Friable periungual papule or granulation tissue, often associated with ingrown nail or targeted cancer therapy; may bleed easily.

list.listitem: Suspect paronychia in a patient who presents with swelling, erythema, and tenderness with or without accompanying fluctuance surrounding the lateral and proximal nail folds. Nail plate elevation may be seen in some cases due to a pus collection.
If the symptoms are present for more than 6 weeks (chronic paronychia), the nail folds may become indurated or hypertrophied, and the nail plate may be thickened or discolored.
Patients usually do not present with constitutional symptoms such as fever or malaise.
It is important to ask about risk factors including high-moisture occupations (eg, dishwasher, bartender) and/or habits such as nail biting or finger sucking, and recent medication use.
Diagnosis is clinical. Culture of the draining pus or scrapings is often unnecessary and should not be routinely performed.
Draining a paronychial abscess should be adequate treatment in most cases.
Ultrasonography can determine presence of an abscess when not clinically evident.

The digital pressure test can confirm the presence of an abscess. The test is performed by having the patient oppose the thumb and affected finger and applying light pressure to the distal volar aspect. A clear demarcation of an abscess if present can be seen.

If patients are not responding to the usual treatment, consider biopsy of the nail fold to rule out malignancies such as squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma. Psoriasis can be diagnosed by clinical appearance or biopsy when needed.
See algorithm in .

Warm soaks or compresses with or without topical antibiotics or steroids are used to treat acute paronychia without abscess or cellulitis. Addition of topical steroids to topical antibiotics decreases time to symptom resolution in acute paronychia without added risk. C

Topical antibiotics include mupirocin, gentamicin or topical fluoroquinolone. Treatment with oral antibiotics, such as clindamycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate, covers most isolated pathogens in acute paronychia, although there is no evidence that oral antibiotics are beneficial following incision and drainage. B
Topical anti-inflammatory agents (steroids or calcineurin inhibitors) and avoidance of irritants are the mainstay of therapy for chronic paronychia. C
Topical steroids are more effective than systemic antifungals in the treatment of chronic paronychia. B

Perform incision and drainage if a fluctuance is noted signifying a pus collection. Eponychial marsupialization or en bloc resection of the proximal nail fold with or without nail plate removal can be performed for recalcitrant chronic paronychias. B

Few RCTs have evaluated the use of topical and oral antibiotics, antifungals, topical steroids, or surgery. There is no evidence that oral antibiotics are preferable to incision and drainage of acute paronychias.

Oral antibiotics should not be used routinely for acute paronychia after adequate drainage. Reserve oral antibiotics for patients with overt cellulitis, systemic illness, immunocompromise, severe infection, failed drainage, or high-risk exposures. When antibiotics are needed, select therapy based on likely pathogens and local resistance patterns. Cephalexin or dicloxacillin may be used for typical MSSA/streptococcal coverage; amoxicillin/clavulanate or clindamycin may be used when oral flora or anaerobes are suspected, such as with nail biting or thumb sucking; doxycycline or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole may be used when MRSA is suspected; ciprofloxacin may be considered when Pseudomonas is suspected.
Topical antibiotics for acute paronychia include mupirocin, gentamicin or a topical fluoroquinolone if pseudomonal infection is suspected.

Topical steroids are more effective than systemic antifungals in the treatment of chronic paronychia. Candida appears to be a common coexisting organism but is not related to the cause or treatment of the disease.

Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment is an alternative topical anti-inflammatory option for chronic paronychia. In a small randomized unblinded trial, tacrolimus 0.1% and betamethasone 17-valerate 0.1% were both superior to emollient alone, and tacrolimus had higher cure/improvement rates than betamethasone.
Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for up to 6 weeks can be used to treat paronychia secondary to epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors.

Incision and drainage using scalpel is recommended if fluctuance is noted. Puncture drainage using hypodermic needle is another acceptable drainage technique. Antibiotics are not necessary following adequate evacuation of abscess associated with acute paronychia.
Eponychial marsupialization with or without nail plate removal can be done in chronic paronychial involvement. The nail plate can be removed when nail irregularities are also noted.

En bloc resection of the proximal nail fold with or without removal of the nail plate was shown to be effective in reducing recurrences in chronic paronychia. Nail plate removal was associated with better surgical outcomes.
Conservative management with warm soaks and/or compresses is thought to provide some relief but has not been systematically studied.
Typical soaks include warm water with Burow's solution (aluminum acetate), 1% acetic acid, chlorhexidine, or dilute povidone-iodine.
Acute paronychia frequently recurs unless the underlying etiology is addressed. C
Chronic paronychia responds slowly to treatment, typically over a period of weeks to months. C
If nail biting or finger sucking is occurring, use the paronychia as a teachable moment to assist the patient in abolishing this habit.
For chronic paronychia, avoid frequent exposure to wet work. If wet work is necessary, suggest waterproof gloves with cotton liners.
Dry hands thoroughly after water exposure.
If fingers are dry and cracking, use moisturizers to prevent new episodes of paronychia.
After surgical drainage, consider performing regular finger soaks or washing the area daily and applying appropriate dressings.

cell.label: Infection/inflammation of the lateral and/or proximal nail folds. Duration?
Acute paronychia likely: swollen, erythematous, tender nail fold, possible fluctuance and warmth.
Common organisms include Staphylococcus aureus (most often), streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides.

Conservative treatment with warm soaks or compresses. Consider antibiotics (clindamycin, amoxicillin/clavulanate). Surgical incision and drainage if fluctuance is noted, rarely removal of nail plate for adequate drainage.
Chronic paronychia likely: swollen, tender, some erythema, induration, nail plate thickened and discolored, no or minimal fluctuance.
Common organisms include Candida albicans (most often), atypical mycobacteria, and Gram-negative rods. Significance of organism unknown.

Avoid irritants, wear cotton gloves under vinyl or nitrile gloves when exposed to water. Topical steroids with oral (ie, griseofulvin) or topical (ie, nystatin) antifungals. Consider eponychial marsupialization or en bloc resection of the affected nail fold with or without removal of the nail plate.
